review: In separate lines the defender loses the rook either through an interception or off the pawn's file before taking the pawn free. The cause of the second cost is not isolated.
The better move also has a searched line that costs a bishop on the same e-pawn.
f5 lets the d-pawn advance to d2 in both weaker lines. Taking it loses a bishop and the alternative yields d1=Q. h6 lets the king approach sooner.
The stronger line also sacrifices a bishop for f2. The played branch can lose in a different way on e1.
Qh3 gives e2 with a threat against the bishop. Taking immediately or after queen checks costs material against the same pawn.
Ne3 c2 Nxc2 loses the knight; other moves let c1=Q. Nxc3 liquidates the original pawn before it advances.
The main line concedes a knight. Excluding the capture finds a different knight-and-pawn position without clear promotion or liquidation of the same pawn.
The independent lines do not establish an early, material-costly interception of the same runner after the played move.
Rxb2 after Qf1 Rc8 concedes the rook. Playing on instead permits bxc1=Q. Qe1 has no comparable cost.
Both sides race to promote and the f-pawn conversion appears only in a lower reply. The root difference is not isolated.
Rf7 g3 and g2 lead to a rook sacrifice; the other legal defence lets g1=Q. Rg8 can give checks and keep the material.
Rg2 allows the f-pawn to reach f2, costing a bishop to take it. Kg2 instead lets that pawn capture and promote.
The e-pawn ties down and costs a rook after Rd5+. Declining to trade on e2 allows e1=Q after a check; Kc1 holds material during the corresponding window.
Ra2 Rc8 leaves Raxb2 answered by Bxb2. The best non-taking defence delays the same cost and Rxb2 on the original turn takes freely.
b5 forces the rook to sacrifice on g2 to stop the two-pawn advance. Playing Ke1 allows g1=Q by the same pawn.
The root line intercepts earlier on d3. The deeper line delays and loses the knight on d2 under different circumstances.

Qe5+ forces a retreat and Rxd2 loses the rook to Qxd2. Declining allows promotion. Rf2 permits promotion too with enough checking activity to retain material and defend.
The same Bxa2 Kxa2 can occur after the better move. A different kingside defence establishes the actual difference.
The stronger and weaker branch compare the resource around e2, but the weaker replies differ between a rook interruption on e2 and a separate knight capture on e1.
Kf1 allows the b-pawn to advance to b2, costing a full rook. Ignoring it permits promotion. Nxb3 instead removes the original pawn for a materially smaller cost.
The same pawn exchange occurs after both moves. The new passer and rook activity determine the difference.
Rc1 permits a d-pawn advance with bishop support. Bxd2 Bxd2 loses a bishop; avoiding that capture permits d1=Q. Be3 keeps an affordable rook capture of d3.
A stronger line also pays for stopping the same c-pawn. The repeated motion of its neighbor and the resulting endgame require additional control.

The capture on d2 is followed by a major exchange. The restricted defence still resolves the pawn and loses to a distinct rook attack.
